     “The latent factor of LLM intelligence”. Follows book/LLM-STYLE-GUIDE.md.
     Rows for papers with no archived fulltext (ilic2024positive, kipnis2025metabench,
     maimon2025iq, and everything from late 2025 on) paraphrase rather than quote;
     numbers there come from abstracts and the paper's own text. Written 2026-09. -->

The evidence is a run of psychometric analyses of model-by-benchmark score matrices, starting in mid-2023 with 29 models on HELM and growing to several hundred models on the Open LLM Leaderboard by 2025, plus a newer line of work that builds one-dimensional capability scales by construction (item response theory). Nearly every study finds a positive manifold and a large first factor; they disagree on whether what remains after it is noise or structure, and the answer moves with the sample of models and benchmarks chosen.

| Date | Source | Setting | Finding | Bearing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023-06 | @burnell2023reveal | 29 LLMs (GPT-3 series, OPT, BLOOM, J1, Cohere, TNLG v2; releases 05/2020–03/2023) on 27 HELM tasks | Mean inter-task correlation r = 0.56. Exploratory factor analysis selects three oblique factors (reasoning, comprehension, core language modelling) explaining 33%, 31% and 17% of variance, 82% cumulative; inter-factor correlations 0.22–0.51. Log model size correlates 0.70 with the first factor. They find "three clear factors, each of which explains a substantial proportion of the variance". | contradicts |
| 2024-01 | @owen2024predictable | BIG-Bench and BBH: 11–18 architectures, 36–44 model sizes, 2M–540B parameters; MMLU incl. GPT-4 | No factor analysis. Aggregate benchmark scores are predicted from scaled compute alone: BBH mean absolute error 3.9pp across a doubling of compute, while individual BIG-Bench tasks have 17pp mean error. "Aggregated benchmarks, averaging over many individual tasks, are much more predictable". | context |
| 2024-02 | @polo2024tinybenchmarks | Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (MMLU has 14K items) | Item response theory: 100 curated items suffice to estimate a model's MMLU score, i.e. the item-by-model matrix is well described by a low-dimensional latent ability. | context |
| 2024-05 | @ruan2024observational | 77 pretrained base models from 21 families on 8 benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, Winogrande, GSM8K, HumanEval, TruthfulQA, XWinograd); instruction-tuned appendix adds GPT-4 and Claude 2 | PCA: PC-1 explains nearly 80% of the variation and is a weighted average of all benchmarks ("general capability"); top 3 PCs ~97% (98.6% for instruction-tuned models). Within each family "the LMs’ PC-1 measure linearly correlates with their log-training FLOPs" with R² > 0.9. Their own method keeps 3 PCs. | supports |
| 2024-07 | @kipnis2025metabench | Six Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks, IRT per benchmark; ICLR 2025 | A sparse item set reproduces total scores; they report "a single underlying common factor whose Spearman correlation with the total score is r= 0.93." Sloth's summary of this work puts the main factor at 80% of the variability. | supports |
| 2024-09 | @ilic2024positive | 591 LLMs on 12 Open LLM Leaderboard tests mapped to fluid reasoning, knowledge, reading/writing and quantitative ability (preprint arXiv 2310.11616, Oct 2023) | Positive manifold and a general factor of ability; in the preferred specification the first factor has a loading of 0.81 (R² 0.66). Ruan et al. cite it as a single factor explaining 85% of Leaderboard performance. Parameter count correlates positively with g, with diminishing returns. | supports |
| 2024-10 | @holm2025danoliteracy | Danish-language benchmark, 8 scenarios (citizenship test, social-media QA, …), open and API models incl. GPT-4 and Claude Opus | One factor explains 95% of scenario-performance variance for Danish. Narrow domain, but the same structure. | supports |
| 2024-10 | @spangher2024generalized | 14 models incl. GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Mistral Large 2, and open models; ~13 benchmarks grouped by hand into three subdomains | No factor analysis; the hierarchy is imposed. Their aggregate (MPG) has raw Pearson correlation 0.9157 with Chatbot Arena and 0.8326 with MMLU. Different models lead different subdomains (heterogeneity noted). | context |
| 2024-12 | @polo2025sloth | 30 model families (53 if base and instruct are split) on 12 benchmarks from Open LLM Leaderboard v1/v2; NeurIPS 2025 | Factor-analytic scaling law. Best predictive fit uses d = 3 skills (reasoning, knowledge, instruction following) with skill correlations 0.12 (reasoning–knowledge), 0.43 (reasoning–IF), 0.20 (knowledge–IF); with d = 2 the two skills correlate 0.61. Skills scale differently: reasoning with size, knowledge with size and tokens. | qualifies |
| 2025-02 | @fodor2025linegoesup | Argument paper, no new data | Benchmark performance is unsuitable as a measure of generalizable cognitive competence; a positive manifold across benchmarks need not indicate a general capability, since many tasks that require intelligence in humans are solvable without it. | context |
| 2025-03 | @zhou2025generalscales | 15 LLMs (GPT-4o, o1, o1-mini, LLaMA 3.1/3.2 1B–405B, DeepSeek-R1 distills) on 63 tasks from 20 benchmarks, 16,108 instances | No factor analysis; 18 rubric-defined demand dimensions annotated per instance instead. Argues population-based factors are sample-dependent: Burnell et al. found 3 factors and Ilić & Gignac 1 on different model samples months apart. | qualifies |
| 2025-07 | @zhang2025trainbeforetest | 61 models from six families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia, GPT-2, Yi) on 24 benchmarks | Under direct evaluation PC1 explains 70% of variance; after a small task-specific fine-tune of every model ("train-before-test") 86%, and 93% within the Qwen family. Cross-benchmark Kendall's τ rises from 0.52 to 0.76. "train-before-test renders the score matrix essentially rank one." PC1 aligns with pre-training compute. | supports |
| 2025-07 | @maimon2025iq | 60 LLMs on 44 benchmarks, exploratory factor analysis | Proposes eight interpretable low-rank factors rather than one; the paper is the strongest multi-factor solution in this set. | qualifies |
| 2025-10 | @epoch2025eci | Epoch Capabilities Index: over three dozen benchmarks stitched into one scale; method in @ho2025rosetta (Dec 2025) | One-dimensional IRT by construction: predicted score = sigmoid(discriminability × (capability − difficulty)). A single capability number per model is then used to track progress and algorithmic efficiency over time. Assumes rather than tests unidimensionality. | context |
| 2026-02 | @kearns2026constructvalidity | Open LLM Leaderboard results | A "structured capabilities" model that lets scale inform capabilities (as in scaling laws) and capabilities inform scores up to measurement error (as in factor models) beats plain latent-factor models on parsimonious fit indices and beats scaling laws at predicting held-out benchmarks. | qualifies |
| 2026-03 | @haznitrama2026neurocognition | 156 models on 10 benchmarks plus three adapted neuropsychological tests (Raven's matrices, spatial working memory, Wisconsin card sorting) | Factor analysis confirms a general factor across the benchmarks; the same models still fail tasks trivial for humans, and performance degrades with images and complexity. | supports |
| 2026-04 | @habba2026growingpains | More than 400 models; multidimensional IRT with anchor items | Between three and eight interpretable skill dimensions explain much of the variance; 100 anchor questions per dataset predict full-evaluation scores within 2–3pp. | qualifies |
| 2026-07 | @hou2026cogarena | 55 open-weight models on 13 cognitive paradigms in 5 groupings (working memory, cognitive control, episodic memory, theory of mind, metacognition) | Nearly all paradigm correlations are positive and a common axis explains about half the variance; the within-grouping advantage is small and sensitive to scoring. | qualifies |

### Gaps

- Almost all factor analyses use open-weight models on the Open LLM Leaderboard family of benchmarks. Frontier proprietary and reasoning models appear only in small samples (14 in Spangher et al., 15 in Zhou et al., an appendix in Ruan et al.), so whether o1-class models break the manifold (math and code up, knowledge flat) has not been measured.
- No study includes agentic, long-horizon or computer-use benchmarks in the score matrix; the manifold is established on short-answer tasks.
- The number of factors is sample-dependent (three in Burnell et al., one in Ilić & Gignac, three in Sloth, eight in Maimon et al.) and no study has tested whether the first factor extracted on one model population predicts a benchmark introduced after those models were trained.
- Nothing compares the LLM factor structure with the human factor structure on the same items; the question the chapter raises about a shared axis remains open.
- The strongest single-factor result (Zhang et al., 86–93%) holds only after equalising task-specific preparation; under ordinary evaluation the same data give 70%.
